I rang Caroline on 9 May and repeated that the book could be completed but Julian had to want it to happen. Then Jamie rang. He said Julian hadn't done much at all and was on 'radio silence'. Jamie, as often on this project, went from being conciliatory to being outraged, and again began to talk about cancelling the contract. 'He's in breach,' Jamie said, 'and if the book is pushed beyond September the publishers around the world will begin cancelling.'

Julian was getting a lot of flak in the press for making Wiki-employees sign contracts threatening them with a £12 million lawsuit if they disclosed anything about the organisation. It was clear he didn't see the problem. He has a notion that WikiLeaks floats above other organisations and their rules. He can't understand why any public body should keep a secret but insists that his own organisation enforce its secrecy with lawsuits. Every time he mentioned legal action against the Guardian or the New York Times, and he did this a lot, I would roll my eyes, but he didn't see the contradiction. He was increasingly lodged in a jungle of his own making and I told Jamie it was like trying to write a book with Mr Kurtz.

Caroline and I made another visit to Norfolk. When we arrived, Julian hugged us both. 'Hello, friend,' he said to me, in a rather formal way – clearly he was gesturing towards my father having died since we last met. The Boateng suit was now grubby and he seemed imprisoned in it. That morning was the point where it all went to another level of ghastliness. He had developed a proper siege mentality. I thought this must have to do with Vaughan and the bad atmosphere at Ellingham Hall, but it was more than that: he had grown to feel his lawyers were the enemy. 'It's disgusting,' he said, when we sat down with Caroline in the drawing room. 'I'm not doing any more work on the book until it's guaranteed that the money is not going to the lawyers.'

'Well, it goes where you want it to go.'

'Disgusting …'

'Nobody pays their full lawyers' bill,' Caroline said.

'I'm not paying it. They've charged me for sitting on a fucking train. I should never have stayed in this country in the first place: I should have flown this jurisdiction.'

'Yes, well, let's …There's a lot of pressure coming from the publishers.'

'I'm on strike. I would rather hack my leg off than let someone fuck me. Do you know how much the whole Max Mosley case cost? £400,000. Do you know how much Tesco v. the Guardian cost? £400,000.'

Caroline: 'How much do you think they should be paid?'

Julian named a figure.

Caroline: 'I think it's going to have to be a bit more than that.'

A week later Julian called to say there 'might be time' to look at the book. The question of time was always bizarre. He said he couldn't meet these impossible deadlines, but while the ship was going down, he didn't miss a single interview, festival, or award ceremony, and he gave fancy reasons for that about feeding his public.

After snow and what seemed like months of rain, the garden at Ellingham Hall was now in full bloom. Nobody was up when I arrived except Vaughan Smith, who opened the door and chatted to me in the kitchen. Vaughan wasn't aware I knew anything about the tension between him and Julian and he understandably fished for detail about how it was all going. I didn't tell him much, though it must have been obvious to him how chaotic things were. He was critical of the people around Julian and said that nearly everyone who came into contact with him was looking to make something. Whether he knew it or not, Smith himself was constantly accused of this, mainly by Julian.

Julian came downstairs laughing and asked me to come with him to the police station. We jumped in the car with Sarah driving and he started excitedly telling me about some people he'd got in Afghanistan who were trying to find out about bias in the Afghan media. It emerged, over a few telephone calls in the car, that the guys in Afghanistan had no contacts and were stuck for something to do, so Julian called Kristinn Hrafnsson, his Icelandic colleague, who tried to drum something up. I later heard Julian call a contact at an activist group to find some people on the ground who might direct his people to a story. It was impressive to see him, on the way to the police station, doing the work of a journalist, and he was good at it. When he wants, he can deploy a kind of ethical charm that gets things done. The woman gave him some numbers and he passed them on to his crew. I say 'crew', because I believe they were the ones doing the cable TV show based on WikiLeaks's work around the world. Along with legal arguments and his fights with various media groups, this was his major preoccupation for months. In the car, we also discussed Alex Gibney, the Oscar-winning documentary film-maker who was slated to do a film on Julian (it came out last year). 'There's a problem of editorial input,' Julian said. 'We want to have some control. But the guy is like quite underhand. He has that arrogance. Then he sent a colleague to talk to us and we're so used to people recording me that we had her frisked for recording devices, and he sent this furious message about what a terrible insult etc.' Julian was always very interested in the movie arrangements being cooked up. 'Movie rights' on the book were always uppermost in his mind. He talked about them a lot, though he also spoke critically of the film-makers who had expressed interest in him. He was happy to dismiss Paul Greengrass, Alex Gibney or Steven Spielberg with a flick of the tongue.

The three of us went to a very pink café in the town and ordered sandwiches and cakes. We sat outside, and Julian got distracted by some young girls walking past. 'Hold on,' he said, and turned his gaze. 'No,' he said. 'It was fine until I saw the teeth.' One of the girls was wearing a brace. When Sarah came back and asked what we were talking about, Julian said he'd been admiring some 14-year-old girls, 'until they came close'. I record this not to show how predatory Julian is – I don't believe he is any more predatory than hundreds of men I've known. It's not that: I tell it to suggest how self-delighted he can be. He doesn't at all see how often his self-delight leads him into trouble. He doesn't understand other people in the slightest and it would be hard to think of a leader who so reliably got everyone wrong, mistaking people's motivations, their needs, their values, their gifts, their loyalty, and thereby destroys their usefulness to him. He was always very solicitous of me when I was with him, but I could tell he responded much more to the fact that I like a joke than to the notion that I was a professional writer. The latter mattered to him for five seconds when he was trying to find a writer to work with, but it was the time-wasting, authority-baiting side that really kept our relationship alive. He thought I was his creature and he forgot what a writer is, someone with a tendency to write things down and perhaps seek the truth and aim for transparency.

He was in a state of panic at all times that things might get out. But he manages people so poorly, and is such a slave to what he's not good at, that he forgets he might be making bombs set to explode in his own face. I am sure this is what happens in many of his scrapes: he runs on a high-octane belief in his own rectitude and wisdom, only to find later that other people had their own views – of w…(truncated for demo)

sections:
This is a list of notable chemical engineers, people who studied or practiced chemical engineering. The main list is those who achieved status in chemical engineering or a closely related field such as management or science. At the foot of the page is a list of people with chemical engineering qualifications who are notable for other reasons, such as actors, sportspeople and authors. These are people sufficiently notable to have an article in Wikipedia. Further articles on chemical engineers would be welcome. See the talk page for suggestions of people who should be added to the encyclopedia (and then to this list).

docs.title: LSR graduate,32,leads her party's UP campaign
sections: LSR graduate,32,leads her party's UP campaign

She seems to be an unlikely choice for the post of general secretary of Apna Dal.

Convent-educated Anupriya Patel,32,an alumnus of Delhis prestigious Lady Shri Ram College who did her masters in psychology from Amity University,Noida,and MBA from Kanpur University,seems to be an unlikely choice for the post of general secretary of the Apna Dal,one of the smaller parties in Uttar Pradesh.

In fact,she herself admits as much,saying she either wanted to set up a business of her own,or take charge of the school in Kanpur established by her father,Sone Lal Patel,who formed the Apna Dal in 1995 as a party of Kurmis,an OBC community.

But when Sone Lal died in a road accident in October 2009,his party colleagues,impressed by Anupriyas speech at the condolence meeting in Lucknow,asked her to take control of the party. She was made general secretary and her mother,Krishna Patel,became the party president.
Since then,Anupriya has been trying to build the party,understand local issues and the caste system,and learn local dialects.

Besides contesting her first election from Rohania constituency of Varanasi,Anupriya is busy campaigning for her party candidates and those of her alliance partners the Peace Party and Bundelkhand Congress.

Saying she had never imagined herself hitting the campaign train,Anupriya adds: Destiny put me in completely opposite circumstances than I had planned or dreamt for myself. I took this responsibility out of love for my father.

She admits that before October 2009,she was not even aware of the mission of Apna Dal because she was sure that this was not the life she wanted. I was married for just 12 days when my father died. I had taught at Amity University and had taken up the administration of the school established by my father, she says.

In the four elections that the Apna Dal contested in the past,it could win only four seats in the 2002 Assembly elections. All the four MLAs later left the party. She hopes to change the partys tally this time. We are concentrating on backwards and tribals, she says.

docs.title: Ovonramwen
sections:
Ovonramwen

- Also called:

- Overami

- Died:

- January 1914, Calabar, Southern Nigeria [now Nigeria]

Ovonramwen (died January 1914, Calabar, Southern Nigeria [now Nigeria]) was a West African ruler who was the last independent oba (king) of the 500-year-old kingdom of Benin (in present-day Nigeria). Ovonramwen tried to maintain his independence in the face of increasing British pressure but was able to delay for only a few years the annexation of his kingdom by the colony of Nigeria.

He was called Idugbowa until he took the title Ovonramwen upon becoming oba. He succeeded to a kingdom much reduced by growing British commercial and colonial encroachment from its greatest extent (c. 1700). He attempted to seal Benin off from Europeans but by 1892 was forced to sign a protection treaty with the British administration. Disputes over trade along the Benin River (1892–94) led to a campaign against Benin; the murder of the British acting consul general in January 1897 precipitated a full-scale military expedition, which captured Benin City in February 1897. Ovonramwen surrendered to the British in August and died in exile.

docs.title: Retinal degenerative diseases: role of dietary supplements in retinal health
sections:
Abstract

Retinal degeneration is a progressive condition that affects the retina, the light-sensitive layer, and deteriorates the inner retinal cells that encompass retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells that are essential for eyesight. Multiple factors including aging, genetic factors, oxidative stress, inflammation, and environmental factors can contribute to retinal degeneration. Retinal degeneration is seen predominantly in Age-related Macular degeneration, Diabetic retinopathy, Glaucoma, and Retinitis pigmentosa that contribute to the leading cause of vision loss. The search for potential and effective therapeutic interventions in the management of retinal degeneration has led to increased interest in dietary supplements, particularly those rich in antioxidant properties. Dietary supplements have been proposed as an ideal source for preventing retinal degeneration, especially supplements containing significant levels of antioxidants that help to reduce the damage to retinal cells. Notably, dietary interventions with carotenoids, flavonoids, alkaloids, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals have shown positive effects in both preclinical and clinical studies by preserving the retinal structure, revitalizing retinal health, delaying disease progression, and improving visual function. To explore this topic further, a systematic search strategy was employed in recent studies that are focused on cell lines, animal models, and human subjects. Ultimately, this review highlights the potential of dietary supplements that should be used as adjunctive therapies alongside comprehensive medical management, aiming to maximize their potential benefits in treating and preventing retinal degeneration.

1 Introduction

The inner surface of an eye is lined with an epithelial tissue called the retina, which is sensitive to light. It collects light and uses it to send electrical impulses to the visual cortex in the brain via the optic nerve (Fig. 1). The multiple layers of retinal cell types that make up the retina include ganglion cells, horizontal, bipolar, amacrine cell bodies, photoreceptor cells like rods and cones, and retinal pigment epithelium, each of which has a specific sort of neural network. Every cell has a specific role to perform in the processing of visual data and crucial for maintaining healthy vision. The specialized region, which is present in the posterior retina's central portion, known as the macula, is responsible for regulating high-resolution visual acuity. The retina may get exposed to a range of environmental stressors, like light-induced damage, ocular pressure, oxidative stress, genetics, protein misfolding, inflammation, cellular signaling, and aging, that may result in the degeneration of the retina [1].

Retinal degeneration is a set of diverse groups of diseases with different etiologies but shares common physiological features due to the uniqueness of retinal tissue. Retinal degeneration is usually recognized by the loss of highly specialized and distinct retinal cells, particularly photoreceptor, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and ganglion cells within the neurosensory retina (Fig. 2) [2]. Photoreceptors and RPE cells are interdependent on each other for the proper differentiation and functioning, and both play critical roles in maintaining vision. These retinal cells work together to perform important functions necessary for the retina to operate properly. RPE and Photoreceptors (rod and cone) cell loss is the final phase and common route in most of the retinal degenerative diseases, which is the primary factor causing blindness worldwide [3]. Retinal degeneration is seen most predominantly in age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and retinitis pigmentosa are the most common types of retinal degenerative diseases increasing globally and contribute to the leading cause for the loss of vision, which are becoming an increasingly prevalent problem in modern society, affecting nearly 34 million people worldwide [4]. Degeneration of RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells are considered as a hallmark for the occurrence of many retinal degenerative diseases. The loss or dysfunction of either the photoreceptor cells or the supporting RPE cells beneath the retina was the main cause of the impairment of vision [5].

Diet, a significant lifestyle factor, has a long-term impact on ocular or eye health and it plays an important key role in averting vision impairment [6]. Dietary intake, especially dietary supplements, provides a beneficial intervention to combat the increasing incidence of retinal diseases like age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy worldwide [6]. The dietary supplement has been reported to have protective effects against the RPE cell and photoreceptor cells, suggesting a positive approach to promoting the survival of the retina. Antioxidants, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective-rich dietary supplements are recommended for the prevention of retinal degeneration and have shown encouraging outcomes throughout the treatment of retinal diseases [7]. Dietary supplements that are involved in the protection or delay of the onset of the disease have received a lot of attention and interest in retinal protection research as a prospective management strategy for ocular degenerative illnesses [8]. Research has shown the value of dietary supplements for neuroprotection in people at risk of retinal degeneration. For instance, dietary supplements that offer active ingredients that are taken in the early stages, help to reduce the progression of the retinal degeneration [9].

2 Review methodology

A literature search was carried out across multiple scientific online databases including PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, Science Direct, Research Gate, and Web of Science. The search term included several keywords like dietary supplements, therapeutic interventions, health benefits, food supplements, retinal degenerative diseases, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy. The search mainly included published articles that are focused on cell lines, animal models, and human subjects that discuss the effect of dietary supplements in the prevention and management of retinal degenerative diseases. A narrative approach was employed to summarize the key findings, highlighting the impact of specific dietary supplements on retinal health. This methodology aims to provide a structural framework for evaluating the role of dietary supplements in retinal health that provided valuable insights into therapeutic interventions for retinal degenerative diseases.

3 Retinal degenerative diseases

Globally, over 2.2 billion individuals grapple with vision impairment, with nearly half of them totaling 1 billion people, facing issues that could have been prevented or are yet to be addressed. The primary culprits behind vision impairment or blindness within this significant demographic are retinal degenerative conditions, such as retinitis pigmentosa, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. The looming threats of population growth, population aging, and shifts in behavior and lifestyle are poised to substantially elevate the risk of vision impairment and blindness on a global scale [10].

3.1 Age-related macular degeneration

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) affects most elderly people, resulting in a gradual decrease or loss of central vision which in turn due to aging, damages the macula (retina's center region), which is composed of tightly packed cone cells [4]. AMD is broadly classified into two different types, namely dry AMD and wet AMD. The dry form is recognized by the buildup of drusen, an extracellular deposit found in between the Bruch membrane's inner layer and the RPE basal lamina, leading to changes in the pigmentation of the RPE, resulting in a yellow spot. The wet form is recognized by Bruch's membrane-choroidal neovascularization [2]. As a result of these changes, RPE cells are lost, which in turn causes photoreceptor death and ultimately impairs central vision. The dry form appears to induce photoreceptor cell loss and deterioration of RPE cells due to accumulation of drusen, while the wet form entirely results in the death of photoreceptors and RPE detachment due to blood vessels growing and leakage of blood into the neural retina that can direct retinal death [11].

3.2 Diabetic retinopathy

Diabetic retinopathy stands as a severe ocular problem arising as a complication of diabetes, and results in the progressive deterioration of the blood vessels located within the retina. The likelihood of its occurrence rises when diabetes persists over time and as well as of the patient's age. Vision loss in individuals with diabetic retinopathy is attributed to macular edema, characterized by capillary leakage, macular ischemia involving capillary occlusion, and the consequences of neovascularization induced by ischemia [12]. Clinically, Diabetic retinopathy can be classified into two types: (1) an early non-proliferative type is recognized by vascular permeability increase, retinal microvascular degeneration within the macula region, basement membrane thickening, and loss of pericytes in the retina, (2) a late proliferative type is recognized by pathological neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal scarring, and retinal detachment [11]. Diabetic retinopathy is mainly associated with RPE dysfunction and the underlying choroidal vasculature, which results in edema of the outer retina [13].

3.3 Glaucoma

Glaucoma delineates a specific category of optic neuropathies marked by their gradual onset in the degeneration of ganglion retinal cells and their related axons within the optic nerve after injury. This process significantly contributes to the deterioration of visual acuity, culminating in eventual blindness. Death of ganglion retinal cells within the inner retinal layer and axonal cells in the optic nerve is a critical component in the pathogenesis of all types of glaucoma [14]. Apart from this, glaucoma not only induces the progressive thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer but also manifests in optic disc cupping. This phenomenon is frequently attributed to elevated intraocular pressure, resulting in the constriction of visual fields [15]. Heightened oxidative stress triggered by elevated hyperglycemia significantly contributes to the progression of glaucoma. Factors such as age, ocular and systemic hypertension, diabetes, and pronounced myopia stand out as noteworthy risk factors influencing the initiation of glaucoma [11].

3.4 Retinitis pigmentosa

Retinitis pigmentosa indeed represents an inherited retinal disorder which varies among other retinal degenerative diseases, that diffusely detoriate and affect the photoreceptor (rod and cone) cells and the RPE function of the retina which is recognized by the progressive loss of vision [2]. Retinitis pigmentosa is classified into three main categories: (i) rod-degenerative, (ii) mixed rod or cone degenerative, and (iii) mertk defects (debris-associated form). Genetic abnormalities in retinitis pigmentosa cause the degeneration of light-sensing photoreceptors, resulting in generalized retinal dystrophy. This initiates the primary deterioration of photoreceptor rod cells, subsequently progressing to the onset of secondary degeneration of the photoreceptor, especially cone cells, resulting in the loss of the central part of the visual field [4]. In the initial phases of retinitis pigmentosa, individuals encounter night blindness and a gradual decline in the peripheral visual field attributable to rod degeneration. As retinitis pigmentosa advances, patients enter later stages characterized by the development of tunnel vision, resulting in profound vision impairment attributed to cone degeneration [16].

4 Dietary supplements and retinal health

Natural substances found in our everyday food like fruits and vegetables help to prevent or treat eye disease in a highly beneficial strategy. The eyes, which make up most of our visual system, need micronutrients including carotenoids, omega-3 fatty acids, flavonoids, vitamins, and trace minerals in order to operate correctly and defend against age-related retinal degenerative diseases. These natural substances exhibit antioxidants, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic, and neuroprotective properties when they are consumed as part of a healthy dietary regimen or as a source of nutritional or dietary supplements (Fig. 3). Dietary strategies that emphasize lifestyle changes are thought to be cost-effective and may be used at the level of public health to reduce modifiable risk factors connected to the most common ocular illnesses and have revealed promising approach over the course of treating degenerative ocular and retinal diseases [6]. Most dietary regimens were granted approval by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to promote the health of the retina. In order to meet the growing demand from customers and patients with vision problems, formulas have been created as dietary interventions. The role of dietary intake, and more especially the effectiveness of several dietary supplements containing carotenoids, flavonoids, alkaloids, amino acids, fatty acids (omega-3), multi-vitamins, and trace minerals in the treatment of ocular-related diseases, has been empirically validated through numerous population-based investigations, randomized controlled trials in participants, prospective cohorts observational studies, retrospective cohorts studies, case–control studies, cellular assays, animal models, and human clinical trials ( (Fig. 4) [17]. The proper dosage, effectiveness, and bioavailability of dietary supplements have been scientifically demonstrated for lowering the risk of eye diseases, including retinal (macular) degenerative diseases and also other eye-related diseases, which were reported in Age-Related Eye Disease Studies (AREDS and AREDS2), this information may assist in selecting an ideal and best dietary supplements in accordance with recommended doses and standard intakes and levels that have been advised by evidence-based research with the goal of improving overall retinal health and preventing diseases connected to the retina [18]. It has revealed the importance of dietary intake, specifically carotenoids, flavonoids, alkaloids, amino acids, fatty acids (omega-3), multivitamins, and trace minerals are involved in the management of retinal health. These categories contain many dietary bioactive compounds. The role of biologically enriched dietary supplements in retinal health is listed in (Table 1) with the recommended dietary allowance. The major dietary supplements have been shown to delay, or in some cases possibly reverse retinal diseases. Because of these findings, scientists are now concentrating on a wide variety of dietary interventions to treat eye conditions including retinal degenerative diseases. The scientific significance of dietary supplements containing natural products and dietary sources emphasizes their pivotal role in supporting the visual system. Specifically, our focus will be on elucidating the approaches by which these dietary interventions contribute to the deceleration of age-related retinal degeneration, providing a nuanced understanding of their potential therapeutic implications in preserving retinal health and physiology.

5 Carotenoids

Carotenoids represent a cohort of lipophilic pigments originating from biogenic substances, categorized into three classes, namely xanthophylls, carotenes, and lycopene. Despite their ubiquitous presence in the natural world, the human diet encompasses approximately 40 carotenoids, with 20 detected in various tissues and biological fluids. A diet rich in these carotenoids has diminished the occurrence of ocular diseases underscoring their potential protective role in ocular health [19]. Carotenoids with proven antioxidant, anti-angiogenic, and anti-inflammatory activities could be of added benefit in treating age-related ophthalmic diseases which include glaucoma, macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy. It indicates that the consumption of dietary supplements containing carotenoids has shown notable therapeutic advantages against several retinal diseases. All carotenoid-based nutrients undergo a sequence of changes through the oxidation process that shields the macular region of the retina [20]. Moreover, carotenoids have demonstrated utility in enhancing visual acuity, promoting ocular blood flow, and facilitating signal transduction processes across the lifespan. There are many different types of carotenoids that were identified and characterized, among them lutein, zeaxanthin, and mezoxanthin are the main carotenoids enclosed within the retina and are named macular pigment carotenoids. These macular carotenoids strongly correlate with the maintenance of retinal health, physiology, and optimal vision [21]. Shortly later, it was discovered that the peripheral regions and central fovea had distinct ratios of lutein to zeaxanthin. Zeaxanthin predominates more in the region of the central fovea while lutein is prevalent in the periphery region. Dietary interventions with carotenoids, especially lutein and zeaxanthin safeguard against the onset of retinal degeneration [22].

6 Flavonoids

Flavonoids, a wide category of polyphenolic compounds, are another family of antioxidants that may have a significant protective effect. They were classified into six primary subclasses based on their structural complexity. These subclasses include flavones, isoflavones, flavonols, flavan-3-ols and flavanones [23]. Flavonoids increase internal antioxidant machinery, decrease inflammatory linked pathways, and improve mitochondrial activities in addition to protecting different ocular inner cell types of the retina from free radical stress-related cell damage. Therefore, flavonoids are therapeutically effective in people with ocular problems [24]. Flavonoids increase the production of neurotrophins. Neuronal factors like neurotrophins are involved in healthy neuronal cell growth and signaling pathways. Additionally, the antioxidant activity of flavonoids has a neuroprotective role and improves the microcirculation of the retina as well as photo-transduction and visual signaling. It has been reported that several flavonoids including anthocyanins, kaempferol, and quercetin have potential neuroprotective and therapeutic roles against neuroinflammation in retinal degenerative diseases. Furthermore, it also demonstrated the positive effects of flavonoids as a therapeutic option for retinal diseases [25]. Dietary interventions with flavonoids and their analogous interlink directly with visual receptors promote the expression levels of rhodopsin and cone opsins of photoreceptors in the retina and modulate visual pigment function [24]. Additionally, flavonoids enhance antioxidant systems and possess antiapoptotic properties that protect not only the retinal ganglion cell death but also recover retinal physiology function. Flavonoids might be useful as preventative agents to protect the retina from deterioration and preserve its function. Therefore, treatment with flavonoids might have beneficial effects and prophylactic value in the prevention of retinal degenerative diseases [24].

7 Alkaloids

Alkaloids constitute a diverse set of bioactive compounds, with a multifaceted biological activity derived primarily from various natural sources. It is commonly used for the treatment of eye disorders. Alkaloids have been used for a very long time in several medications in the field of ophthalmology. In the eye, alkaloids can act as antioxidants, anti-angiogenic, and anti-inflammatory agents [26]. It is known that alkaloids may act as antioxidants, that inhibit free radicals, thereby protecting and shielding the neuro-retinal cells from oxidative stress-related harm. It can also act as an anti-angiogenic that protects the retina by inhibiting angiogenic responsible factors that lead to new blood vessel formation. It can be beneficial in treating retinal diseases like diabetic-related retinopathy and retinal or macular degeneration. Alkaloids can function as anti-inflammatory agents resulting in the downregulation of pro-inflammatory factors, which can help to protect the eye from damage due to inflammation. Alkaloids are anticipated to be beneficial in the management of conditions linked to the neovascularization of the retina. Alkaloids are successfully used for reducing high intraocular pressure, particularly in case of severe visual neuropathy [27]. Alkaloids with medicinal properties would provide a potential innovative therapy and are often utilized as medications; among various alkaloids, physostigmine and pilocarpine are commonly used with the purpose of treating retinal related degenerative diseases. Physostigmine is used to treat glaucoma. It works by increasing the fluid outflow from the eye, which helps to lower intraocular pressure. Pilocarpine is also derived from a plant, and it is used to treat glaucoma and other eye conditions that cause blurry vision. Ergot alkaloids are applied to treat diverse ocular/retinal diseases, as in diabetic retinopathy, uveitis, and age-related macular degeneration [26].

8 Amino acids

Amino acids are organic compounds that are vital to a number of biological activities in humans. They serve as the structural components of proteins, which are necessary for the growth, maintenance, and repair of all tissues. There are 20 amino acids, and each one has a unique side chain, that gives it its unique characteristics. The body can synthesize most of the amino acids from other molecules, but nine of them are essential amino acids that can be taken from the diet. Amino acids are important crucial nutrients, actively participate in diverse biological processes, and their pivotal roles encompass protein synthesis, glucose metabolism, and lipid metabolism, moreover within metabolic tissues associated with aging-related conditions. Notably, recent findings underscore the significant correlation between amino acids and neuroprotection, anti-oxidative mechanisms, and anti-inflammatory responses within the retina [28]. Amino acid levels have been quantitatively assessed in most ocular tissues and have been described separately for each retina associated cells. The ocular tissues of the eye, both neuronal and non-neural, are functionally diverse and may have variable amino acids [29]. All proteins in the dietary supplement are made up of different compositions of amino acids, which are also merely plentiful. Amino acids such as glutamine, aspartate, gamma amino butyric acid, taurine, proline, and glycine exhibited evidence of functioning as neurotransmitters in neural tissues, including the retina [30]. These active amino acids serve as a nitrogen source for the retina and RPE cells/choroids and support retinal metabolism [31]. Therefore, slight changes in the ratios of amino acids present in the retina cause retinopathy, particularly diabetic related retinopathy and macular degeneration associated with age. These initiatives are intended to advance our understanding of amino acids at the basic level in order to facilitate new insights and studies on retinal health and diseases [32].

9 Fatty acids

Essential fatty acids which are taken from a healthy diet nourish our visual system. There are several dietary sources that provide fatty acids: for instance, it is classified into short-chain and long chain fatty acid (omega-3) named as alpha-linoleic acid, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) [6]. Fatty acids are now a popular dietary supplement that are being thoroughly researched for their health advantages, successfully lower demyelination of axon in optic nerve. Fatty acids supplementation in the diet suppresses metabolic pathways linked to the etiology of degenerative disorders in the retina. Dietary interventions with a complete and balanced mixture of fatty acids, slowed down inflammation, macrophage infiltration, and gliotic processes in the cells of the retina. In addition, the diet supplement rich in fatty acids resulted in a neuroprotective impact by avoiding retinal ganglion cell death associated with optic neuritis [33]. However, a pilot study investigated that EPA-rich omega-3 fatty acids supplementation provides a mean to improve both objective and subjective vision and prevent further vision loss, in patients with moderate to severe dry age-related macular degeneration [34]. The National health and nutrition examination survey revealed that higher dietary intake of DHA, DPA, and EPA is linked to reductions in the early stages of any AMD. The study corroborated earlier findings showing that patients with AMD benefit from omega-3 PUFAs [35]. The dietary supplementation involving a combination of fatty acids effectively countered the upregulation of markers associated with the complement system, angiogenesis, and inflammation. This observed effect extended to both retinas of the ocular and the RPE/choroid complex. The supplementation and/or intervention demonstrated a regulatory impact on these biological processes, indicating a potential role within the ocular tissues. Dietary supplements with fatty acid mixtures restore the shortage of bioactive lipids, which mostly contribute to macular related illness. Dietary supplements with a well-balanced blend of fatty acids prevented thickness decrease of the outer nuclear retinal layer, development of gliosis, and macrophage infiltration in the retina. Additionally, the fatty acid supplement had a neuroprotective impact by reducing inflammatory activities and avoiding retinal cell death. The available findings indicate that fatty acids could be a helpful dietary supplement to stop or slow the course of retinal dysfunction and it is effective in preventing the dry age-related macular degeneration-like pathological symptoms that are characteristic of retinal disease [36].

10 Vitamins

Vitamins are vital biological substances that the body needs in trace amounts for normal body function, growth, and development. Vitamins are integral to numerous biochemical functions in the human body, serving as indispensable constituents for sustaining optimal health. Vitamins are categorized into two principal groups: fat-soluble (vitamins—A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (vitamins—B, C). Vitamin, as an antioxidant, has a positive impact on the retina's biochemistry and structural aspects. Vitamins are primary dietary components shown closely associated with the prevention of retinal degeneration [37]. It has investigated the potential link between antioxidant vitamins and macular degeneration associated with aging, albeit few of them have particularly dependent on supplementation, because people who regularly consume supplements or eat a diet high in antioxidant vitamins differ from those who do not in many ways [38]. Efficient vitamins for lowering the risk of retinal degenerative related diseases are vitamins A, C, and E aid in minimizing the harmful effects of oxidants. Vitamin A is particularly important for the health of RPE cells, which are crucial for maintaining retinal physiology. Vitamins B, C, D, and E also have antioxidant properties and can contribute to the overall health of the retina. It is recommended to consume a healthy diet that includes a dietary source rich in these vitamins [39]. In addition, retinal degeneration may be prevented by leading a healthy lifestyle and eating a healthy diet that includes multivitamins or another vitamin supplementation. Vitamins may also be beneficial in potentially reducing the risk of retinal degeneration by approximately 25% with vitamin supplementation. Many clinicians recommend dietary supplements to lessen the progression of retinal related degeneration and support overall eye health [40].

11 Minerals

Minerals are essential nutrients required to perform their basic functions. There are two types of minerals,namely macro minerals and trace minerals. Minerals as micronutrients are crucial in maintaining retinal health and physiology. These minerals are found in high concentrations in certain retinal cells with more energy requirements. It has been shown that abnormal mineral concentrations may harm retinal cells. However, the importance of trace minerals in retinal health, physiology and disease relies on both in terms of their quantities and distribution, which are tightly controlled by linked metabolic processes. They participate in diverse retinal processes, including phototransduction, the visual cycle, neurotransmission, cellular antioxidant defense, retinal homeostasis, detoxification, and intricate associations with metabolic pathways. The concentration of minerals required for compartmentalization, and oxidation or reduction states are directly or indirectly influenced by these processes, and they are intricately bound to proteins and other molecules, playing a regulatory role in retinal physiology [41]. It's important to note that while minerals are important for eye health, they should be consumed in moderation. Diet and dietary supplements rich in minerals are essential for maintaining retinal physiology and health. Iron, zinc, and copper are necessary trace components that perform specific retinal activities, in the construction and physiology of the retina [42]. It allows vitamins to travel from the liver to the retina to produce melanin, a pigment that protects the eyes. Zinc is one of the most important minerals, as it is a necessary component of several enzymes that are required for retinal metabolism and health. Dietary rich source of mineral supplementation, when taken with vitamins minimize the loss of visual acuity and even halt the age-related disease progression including retinal degeneration [42].

12 Exploring other dietary supplements in retinal health

The Exploration of other dietary supplements in promoting retinal health has evolved significantly, driven by pioneering research that has established the connection between specific nutrients and ocular well-being, which are responsible for the management of retinal degenerative diseases. This section highlights key studies and hypotheses that have shaped the understanding of various dietary supplements, including melatonin, saffron, curcumin, and ginkgo biloba in the context of retinal degenerative diseases [6]. Melatonin has attracted attention for its potential therapeutic effects on ocular diseases. It is synthesized in various ocular tissues and plays a crucial role in regulating retinal health. Studies suggest that melatonin has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties, which may help prevent retinal injury under intraocular hypertension conditions. Exogenous melatonin supplementation has been shown to improve outcomes in age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy by reducing oxidative stress and promoting retinal cell survival [43]. Saffron, as a potential dietary supplement for eye health, suggests that it may protect against oxidative stress in retinal cells. A clinical study found that daily supplementation with saffron led to significant improvements in visual acuity and delayed the progression among individuals with dry macular degeneration. The active compounds in saffron, such as crocin, crocetin, and safranal, exhibit antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, making saffron a promising candidate for supporting retinal health [44]. Curcumin is recognized for its potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Research has demonstrated that curcumin can mitigate oxidative stress and reduce the levels of inflammatory markers in various retinal disorders, including diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration. Additionally, curcumin was considered as a valuable adjunct therapy for managing retinal diseases [45]. Ginkgo biloba has been studied for its neuroprotective effects due to its ability to improve blood flow and reduce oxidative stress. Some studies suggest that Ginkgo biloba extract may help improve visual function in patients with glaucoma by enhancing retinal blood flow and protecting against neuronal damage. The hypothesis here posits that Ginkgo biloba may serve as an adjunct treatment for various retinal diseases [46]. This emerging hypothesis highlights the need for further investigation into novel dietary supplements in preventing retinal degenerative diseases. Continued research will further elucidate these relationships, enhancing our understanding of how nutrition can influence ocular health.

13 Conclusion

The crucial role of dietary interventions in the retinal cells holds a promising approach to retinal degeneration. The studies reviewed in this article suggest that certain dietary supplements, such as carotenoids, flavonoids, fatty acids, alkaloids, amino acids, vitamins, and minerals may have beneficial effects on retinal health and perhaps halt the progression of retinal degeneration. Carotenoids, such as lutein and zeaxanthin, are a natural pigment that exists in the macula region of the retina. These carotenoids have demonstrated the ability to improve visual function, raise the macular pigment density, and reduce the risk of retinal disease progression. Flavonoids are a diverse group of bioactive compounds that are recognized for their antioxidant as well as anti-inflammatory properties. Several flavonoids, including quercetin and resveratrol, are responsible for their beneficial effects on retinal health. Alkaloids such as physostigmine and pilocarpine are frequently used in the management of retinal-related diseases. Amino acids are highly related to neuroprotection in the retina. Amino acids like glutamine, aspartate, taurine, proline, and glycine demonstrated the ability to function as signaling components in neuronal tissues, including the retina. Omega-3 fatty acids, specifically EPA and DHA, have been associated with maintaining retinal structure and improving visual function. Vitamins and minerals, like vitamin A, C, and E, zinc, and selenium, have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and retinal protective effects that may benefit retinal health. However, it is important to emphasize that dietary supplements are recommended for revitalizing retinal health and in the management of retinal degeneration.

docs.title: 315 Fictional Literary Magazines (Digital & Print) to Publish Your Work & For Your Reading Pleasure
sections:
If you wish to find small batches of creative works from talented individuals from all walks of life, all over the world, regardless of their level of experience – Literary Magazine is the absolute venue of which you should explore. This compilation is a little bit different in the sense that it's actually for both readers and writers. As obvious as it is for readers, writers from any skill level will find the below list extremely beneficial as these literary magazines accept your work to be included in their magazine. Out of this huge list of 315 awesome magazines, you'll find all kinds of topics, approach, objectives, missions and even the medium on how they publish their magazines.

Some will keep them digital, some will even print them (or even both). Some will require a small fee to process your submission(s), some will accept it for free indefinitely. Editions will be published annually, semi-annually or even quarterly depending on how these wonderful people want to get them out. Some will even sell these magazines and then distribute the revenue equally among all the contributors, some will just give them out for free for that well needed exposure for all new writers. Nonetheless, the level of creativity and collaboration that you'll see within this circle is simply mind-blowing.

You'll find all kinds of fictions, poetries, artworks and even podcasts within this jungle of treasure. We would also like to bring to your attention that some of these publications or companies many not be active anymore as they have stopped, but all of their published works are still available in their archive or even to be purchased. We do really hope that both readers and authors would take advantage of this huge list and do have a great time!

Feel free to share this post with your friends, get in touch with us, continue to read, keep on writing and reach that daily word quota and most importantly – stay safe!

Have a good one guys.

315 Fictional Literary Magazines (Digital & Print) to Publish Your Work & For Your Reading Pleasure

- 2 Elizabeths – A Literary Magazine with a Heart for Community.

- 34thParallel Magazine – Indie Litmag Digital & Print.

- 3Elements Review – 3Elements Literary Review is a quarterly, online literary journal founded in Chicago in 2013, now based in Des Moines, IA. 3Elements publishes fiction, nonfiction, poetry, art, and photography.

- A Quiet Courage – A Journal of Microfiction and Poetry in 100 Words or Less.

- A Velvet Giant – A genreless Literary Journal.

- Agonia – Poetry, prose, essays, comments, poems – International Culture and Literature.

- Alligator Juniper – A literary magazine from the high desert of Arizona.

- Ambit Magazine – Ambit is a 96-page quarterly literary and art magazine. It is created in London, published in the UK, and read internationally. It's available through subscription, in selected bookshops, and in libraries worldwide.

- American Chordata – American Chordata is a literary and arts magazine that's beautiful to look at; packed with bright voices in fiction, essay, poetry, art, and photography; and curated by weirdos who love brave new writing as much as you do.

- American Letters & Commentary – American Letters & Commentary, Inc. is an eclectic, nonprofit literary publisher dedicated to promoting innovative and challenging writing in all forms.

- Angie's DIARY | Online Writing Magazine – Literary guest post blog and online magazine for readers and writers of essays, op-eds, short stories, articles on health, the arts, lifestyle, humanism, poetry.

- Antioch Review – The Antioch Review, a small independent literary magazine founded in 1941 in a small town in the cornfields of Ohio, is one of the oldest, continuously publishing literary magazines in America. Publishing essays, fiction, and poetry from promising and prominent authors.

- Antiphon poetry magazine – Antiphon poetry magazine was founded in 2011 and is edited and produced in the UK by Rosemary Badcoe and Noel Williams. Issues 1 to 24 can be found in their website, together with links to hear many of the poems reading their work.

- Apple Valley Review – The Apple Valley Review is an online literary journal. It is published twice annually, once in spring and once in fall. Each issue features a collection of poetry, short fiction, and essays.

- ARDOR Literary Magazine – ARDOR Literary Magazine is an online tri-annual publication featuring original short fiction, nonfiction, poetry and artwork.

- Asinine Poetry – Asinine Poetry is the journal of asinine poetry, a quarterly publication of asinine poetry, poetry that is, shall they say, asinine.

- At Length – At Length is a venue for ambitious, in-depth writing, music, photography, and art that are open to possibilities shorter forms preclude. They create ways for readers, listeners, and viewers to interact with noteworthy long work, and other publications have noticed.

- Atlas and Alice Literary Magazine – Among their favorite intersections are pieces that resist genre classification (think prose poems, think flash fiction, think…), crossovers between the arts and sciences, opposites attracting, likes repelling, anything that confronts and, in confronting, reveals.

- autolycus – An utterly independent literary journal, created by Genie Cartier and Emilio Aldrich. They aim to publish talented unknown writers, and sell the journal online and by consignment.

- Avalon Literary Review – The Avalon Literary Review is dedicated to publishing noteworthy works of poetry, short fiction and personal essays.

- B O D Y – B O D Y is an international online literary journal. They publish the highest quality poetry and prose from emerging and established writers. They also showcase contemporary artworks and photography.

- Bacopa Literary Review – Bacopa Literary Review is published by the Writers Alliance of Gainesville annually. Unique fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.

- BALLOONS Lit. Journal – A children and young adults literary magazine – where creativity, imagination, weirdness, adventures, and poetry play.

- Baltimore Review – A literary hub of diverse writing and promote the work of emerging and established writers. In 2012, The Baltimore Review began its new life as a quarterly, online literary journal.

- Bare Fiction Magazine – UK Literary magazine and independent press publishing new poetry, fiction, short story, flash fiction, and short plays three times a year in print and regularly online.

- Bartleby Snopes – Short Story and Fiction Publisher. Bartleby Snopes no longer publishes new stories but the stories they accepted during their 9 years of publication will remain permanently archived on this website.

- Beloit Fiction Journal – The Beloit Fiction Journal publishes the best in contemporary short fiction. Traditional and experimental narratives find a home in their pages. They publish new writers alongside established writers.

- Bennington Review – Bennington Review is a national biannual print journal of innovative, intelligent, and moving poetry, fiction, creative nonfiction, and film writing, housed at Bennington College.

- Beorh Weekly – The magazine of peculiar literature.

- Berkeley Fiction Review – UC Berkeley's oldest prose journal, publishing short fiction since 1981.

- Big Fiction – BIG FICTION Magazine celebrates the long story – generous, transportive, and a little wild. They celebrate the spirit of the long essay: curious, self-aware, and free. Publishes ambitious fiction and nonfiction twice a year.

- Black Denim Lit – Black Denim Lit welcomes thoughtful writers, new and established. They are accepting submissions through Submittable.

- Black Heart Magazine – Publishes the best in short-form modern literature, across all genres. Currently they publish short fiction only (no poetry, no essays).

- Black Scat Review – A small, independent press dedicated to publishing books of sublime art & literature, absurdist fiction, dada, surrealism, pataphysics, erotica, and works in translation.

- Blackbird – An online journal of literature and the arts. Founded in 2001 as a joint venture of the Virginia Commonwealth University Department of English and New Virginia Review, Inc.

- Blotterature – Blotterature is an online literary magazine, started in August 2013 by a few Region Rats who came together via The Literary Underground, along with late night poetry and debauchery.

- Blue Collar Review – The Blue Collar Review is a quarterly journal of poetry and prose published by Partisan Press. Their mission is to expand and promote a progressive working class vision of culture that inspires us and that moves us forward as a class.

- Blue Lyra Review – Blue Lyra Review aims to unite writers and artists from a diverse array of backgrounds, paying special homage to the voices of Jewish writers and those from other underrepresented communities. They accept poetry, nonfiction, translations book reviews and artistic images.

- Bookforum Magazine – Contributors have taken on an array of topics, writing essays, columns, and reviews about fiction, history, fashion, feminism, current events, policy, bestsellers, fashion, film, music, pop culture, and personal obsessions.

- Bop Dead City – Bop Dead City was an independent, quarterly literary magazine. They are permanently closed as of December 7, 2017, but you may still find their previous publications online.

- Boston Accent Lit – Boston Accent Lit aims to showcase work that is daring and innovative, as well as to provide a platform for underrepresented voices. They publish quality work by both emerging and established artists.

- Brain, Child: The Magazine for Thinking Mothers – An award-winning literary magazine dedicated to motherhood. Each issue contains personal essays, a short story, poetry, debates, book reviews and news.

- Brick, A Literary Journal – Brick is an international literary journal, based out of Toronto, which prizes the personal voice and celebrates life, art, and the written word.

- Brilliant Flash Fiction – Submissions are open 365 days a year, and there are no reading fees. Brilliant Flash Fiction welcomes submissions from writers at all levels of experience.

- Broad Street Magazine – Broad Street is an interdisciplinary magazine of letters and art, begun at Virginia Commonwealth University in 2012 and now independently operated. Narrative essays, researched reflection, experimental truth-telling, photo essays, belles lettres, poetry, and all forms of visual art come together here.

- Broad! (A Gentlelady's Magazine) – Broad! is a online literary semiannual that publishes exclusively writers and artists who identify as women, trans*, or outside the gender binary. Female, trans*, and genderqueer writers are severely underrepresented in literary publications today, and we hope to help change that. They accept poetry, fiction, creative nonfiction (particularly personal essays and nonfictional narrative), photography, and visual art.

- Buck off Magazine – Online literary magazine where Writing Meets Attitude. After 5 years and 10 editions, Buck Off Magazine has ended its publications, but is still available until the end of time.

- Cactus Heart – Cactus Heart was a literary magazine founded by Sara Rauch in 2012. From Cactus Heart's first issue to its last in 2016, the magazine was dedicated to publishing fiction, poetry, nonfiction, and visual art that was sharp, devastating, and vulnerable.

- Camroc Press Review – Not currently active but have a wide range of submissions from a group of authors available on their website.

- Cardinal Sins – Saginaw Valley State University's (SVSU) arts and literature publication. They publish writing and artwork/photography twice a year.

- Carve Magazine (11th) – Diverse community that engages in conversations with writers in print, digital, and online. Publishing honest fiction, poetry, nonfiction, and more.

- Cecile's Writers Magazine – Founded in 2012, Cecile's Writers Foundation published their first magazine in July of 2013. They have now published dozens of literary work by writers who all have one thing in common: interculturalism.

- Chagrin River Review – Chagrin River Review aims to publish the best contemporary short fiction and poetry available to readers today. Chagrin River Review seeks flash fiction, and poetry that explore the human experience and reveal emotional truth.

- China Grove – China Grove is a journal for and about writing. It is designed to give a look at the best of what's out, a look back at the history of the best writers of the past, and to juxtapose that with the new writers of the future.

- Cleaver Magazine – Cleaver is a Philadelphia-based online magazine that provides a platform for underrepresented writers and artists producing work of the highest quality.

- Clementine (Unbound) – Clementine Unbound is an online-only poetry journal/blog edited and published on a weekly schedule by G. F. Boyer.

- CLOCKHOUSE – A national literary journal published by Clockhouse Writers' Conference in partnership with Goddard College.

- Coffin Bell – A journal of dark literature.

- Coldnoon: A Quarterly of Travel Poetics – International Journal of Travel Writing & Travelling Cultures.

- Compose: A Journal of Simply Good Writing – Compose: A Journal of Simply Good Writing is a biannual, online publication that features work by both established and emerging writers of fiction, poetry, and nonfiction.

- Concho River Review – Concho River Review is a biannual literary journal published by the Department of English and Modern Languages at Angelo State University. Since its inception, CRR has prided itself on publishing some of the finest short fiction, nonfiction, and poetry from both emerging and established authors.

- CONSEQUENCE magazine – An International Literary Magazine Focusing on the Culture and Consequences of War.

- Contraposition – Contraposition is a digital and print based literary magazine. Our print volumes are released biannually and sometimes carry a theme. Their web selection is a rolling, non-themed anthology.

- Contrary Magazine – Contrary® was founded in 2003 at the University of Chicago by students and alumni of Chicago's Master of Arts Program in the Humanities. It now operates independently and without a thought of profit on the South Side of Chicago and publishes writers from throughout the world.

- Cowboy Jamboree – Rag & press dedicated to grit lit and rural writing with rough edges, fiction or non.

- Crab Fat Literary Magazine – Crab Fat Magazine is founded on the principles of inclusive & diverse writing/publishing. This means we actively seek work from marginalized people. Crab Fat accepts submissions on a rolling basis. They're interested in flash fiction, poetry, creative non-fiction (lyric essay & memoirs are some of our favorites), visual art, & book reviews from small indie presses.

- Creation and Criticism – Creation and Criticism (CC), which is a quarterly international peer-reviewed refereed English e-journal, aims at providing an opportunity to the researchers and scholars for sharing their creative and critical views through poems, plays, fiction, interviews, book reviews and research articles.

- Cumberland River Review – A quarterly online publication of new poetry, fiction, essays, and art. The journal is produced by the department of English at Trevecca Nazarene University, in Nashville, Tennessee, and welcomes submissions from both national and international writers and artists.

- CutBank – CutBank publishes two print issues a year of compelling poetry, fiction, and literary nonfiction by established writers and new voices alike.

- Dappled Things – Catholic literary magazine – A quarterly journal of ideas, art, and faith.

- Dark Futures – They're interested in flash and short science fiction stories, preferably stories with some form of dark or cynical themes. They also love cyberpunk, grimdark (of the sci-fi variety, futuristic dystopian, and post apocalyptic stories. Space opera and other forms of science fiction are also welcome and some element of darkness, such as a powerful villain character (think Darth Vader) will increase their chance of acceptance.

- Del Sol Review – Del Sol Review was started in 1998. It was first known as "Editor's Picks" and served the purpose of highlighting select work from print journals on WebdelSol.Com. DSR has published twenty issues and shows no signs of stopping.

- Delmarva Review – Founded in 2008, Delmarva Review is a literary journal dedicated to the discovery and publication of compelling new fiction, poetry, and creative nonfiction from emerging and established writers. We publish annually, and promote various literary and educational events to inspire readers and writers who pursue excellence in the literary arts.

- Dime Show Review – They accept fiction, flash fiction, ten-word stories and poetry.

- drafthorse – drafthorse is a biannual online publication of fiction, creative nonfiction, poetry, visual narrative, and other media art where work, occupation, labor—or lack of the same—is in some way intrinsic to a narrative's potential for epiphany.

- Dreamers Creative Writing – Dreamers Creative Writing is dedicated to writing that is from the heart.

- Drunk Monkeys – A monthly online magazine devoted to literature & film. Featuring short fiction, flash fiction, poetry, creative non-fiction, film reviews, interviews, & podcasts.

- Duende – Duende is the all-online literary journal of the BFA in Writing degree-track at Goddard College. They publish one issue per year in the fall, along with a themed feature issue each spring. They also publish original content at the beginning of every month, as well as monthly book reviews by their editors.

- DUMAS de Demain: The French Literary Magazine – Dumas de Demain, a French Literary Magazine is a website created for emerging writers to show the world their talents. They accept poems, fables, plays, tales or comic strips.

- Earthen Lamp Journal – A listing of over 600 magazines of fiction stories, compiled over 10 years. Some of these listings are older, and we are doing our very best to bring you up to date listings. Submissions are totally free.

- Eastern Iowa Review – Eastern Iowa Review was established in 2014 as an offshoot of Port Yonder Press which no longer publishes books.

- El Portal – Eastern New Mexico University's literary magazine, El Portal, offers a unique venue for the work of writers, artists and photographers.

- Elan Literary Magazine – Élan is an international student literary magazine originally published by the English Department at Douglas Anderson School of the Arts in 1986. Each year a staff of high school juniors and seniors, fueled by a passion for the written word and artistic expression, continues the tradition of publishing a word-class literary publication.

- Elbow Pads – Elbow Pads is an annual literary magazine publishing prose, poetry, and photography. Elbow Pads favor the candid outlook of creative individuals but we can deal with the mysterious types, too.

- Embark: A Literary Journal for Novelists – Embark is a literary journal designed for novelists and featuring exclusively novel beginnings—those crucial first pages that must engage the reader's attention and often receive more polishing than any other part of the book.

- Embers Igniting – An editing service whose goal is to partner with writers, to focus on the process of writing by helping authors improve their craft, and to foster and promote a community of writers who are seeking to refine their work.

- Epiphany, a literary Journal – Travellers to South East Asia and India see bicycles loaded up with such an array of miscellanea they enter the mind and become impossible objects. They are connected to the earth, but only incidentally. They glide above it. They are full of magic.

- Episodic Magazine – Episodic is dedicated to the jigsaw-ness of life – the way it fits together – the big picture made up of many meaningful smaller pictures.

- Eunoia Review – Eunoia Review is a Singapore-based online literary journal committed to sharing the fruits of 'beautiful thinking'. Each day, we publish two new pieces of writing for your reading pleasure.

- Exclusive – You will find publishers, magazines, articles, lists, individual authors, stories, reviews, contests, books. There should be something for everyone from people wanting to get an idea of what innovative literature is, to people who make it their careers.

- Exposition Review – Exposition Review is an independent, multi-genre literary journal that publishes narratives by new, emerging, and established writers in the genres of fiction, nonfiction, poetry, stage & screen, experimental, visual art, and comics.

- Fairies and Fairy Tales – Stories are beautiful and the best stories come from great writers who have the freedom to write or thousands of years of culture. This is why they have started a magazine dedicated to bringing these two types of stories together.

- Fantasy Scroll Magazine – Fantasy Scroll Magazine was a first monthly, then quarterly e-zine that was published between 2014 and 2016. Although it has stopped, its archive lives on the interwebs.

- Far Off Places – Far Off Places is a magazine featuring creative writing and illustration which ran from 2013 to 2018. Despite being based in Edinburgh, they spread their loving tentacles over Europe and across the Atlantic. Their mission in life is to make you laugh, ponder, and wince.

- Felled Limbs – Everyone lacks something. At Felled Limbs, we are not interested in looking for the things that are lost, and we have no desire to replace them. Instead, we spend our time staring into the empty spaces, and learning how to let go.

- Fiction International – Fiction International is the only literary journal in the United States emphasizing formal innovation and social activism. Each issue revolves around a theme and features a wide variety of fiction, nonfiction, indeterminate prose, and visuals by leading writers and artists from around the world.

- Fiction War Magazine – Fiction Wars are seasonal writing competitions giving modern fictioneers 3 DAYS to create a short masterwork. These three days are called the 3-DAY FICTION WAR. All entries must be 1000 words or fewer.

- filling Station – filling Station Magazine is a literary and arts magazine publishing innovative poetry, fiction, non-fiction (creative non-fiction, reviews, articles, interviews, live event reviews, photo essays, etc), and presenting a featured visual artist each issue.

- FishFood Magazine – FishFood Magazine is an independent literary and arts magazine dedicated to all forms of creative expression and talent. FishFood encourages self-expression from daily life through art.

- Five 2 One Magazine – FIVE:2:ONE is primarily dedicated to the transgressive, the progressive and the experimental. That is to say that we like the unexplored waters. We love the hell out of the cross-genre scientists, the visual inventors,plucky linguists, non-narratives narrators, and especially the experimental weird babies.

- Fjords Review – Fjords Review was founded in 2010 by John Gosslee. The magazine has featured a number of editors and guest editors and is housed in New York Public Library's Helen Bernstein Periodicals and Journals Library, Southbank Centre's Poetry Library and Poet's House Special Collections Literary Journals permanent collections.

- Flash Fiction Online – Flash Fiction Online – short stories for the modern reader.

- Flyleaf Literary Journal – Based in Chicago, Flyleaf Journal publishes exceptional short fiction written by both emerging and established writers. Each issue they publish is comprised of a single short story and an accompanying illustration designed by a graphic collaborator.

- FORTH Magazine – They explore, expose, and celebrate this forward-moving, always-evolving creative energy that makes us human. - The Washington Pastime – The Washington Pastime, LLC was founded in 2011 as a free electronic and print publication based in Washington, DC committed to publishing the best in literary and genre fiction. They strive to publish only the most provocative and moving literature we come across.

- the Wildwood Reader – Features the work of new and emerging writers. We provide an outlet for writers that have work to share with readers that appreciate and enjoy reading short fiction.

- The Winter Anthology – An argument that the finest works of contemporary art are systems balanced at the edge of chaos, at the highest points of equilibrium between complexity and clarity. An electronic collection until sufficient material for a print version accumulates.

- The Woven Tale Press – The Woven Tale Press, the web's premier online literary and fine art magazine, is also a hub for writing and visual arts, bringing together notable artists and writers seeking to share their work more broadly with communities actively in quest of unique voices and compelling perspectives.

- The Zodiac Review – The Zodiac Review was launched in 2011 by writers/editors Daniel VanTassel and Brian Wright to provide a quality magazine for new, emerging and established writers of "literary/genre" fiction, the merger of literary fiction and any genre that cares to join it.

- Thrice Fiction – Published three times a year, Thrice Fiction is filled with stories, art, and a few surprises from a variety of talented contributors. But the best part? It's absolutely FREE!

- Tin House – The first issue of Tin House magazine arrived in the spring of 1999, the singular lovechild of an eclectic literary journal and a beautiful glossy magazine. A literary magazine for the many passionate readers who are not necessarily literary academics or publishing professionals.

- TreeHouse – TreeHouse is an online magazine filled with works of fiction, poetry, art, photography, film, and music from up-and-coming and established artists, as well as artist interviews and guest blog posts.

- TSR: The Southampton Review – The Southampton Review has been publishing compelling writing and art since 2007. Their goal is to create a literary journal filled with debut, emerging, and established authors; a literary journal that is inclusive of marginalized voices; a literary journal in which our readers will find themselves represented.

- TWJ Magazine – TWJ Magazine is an exciting resource for bringing news of wholesome entertainment to the attention of avid readers, movie-goers and music lovers.

- Typehouse Literary Magazine – A Northwest fiction, poetry, non-fiction and art magazine.

- Unbroken – Unbroken is a quarterly online journal that seeks to showcase prose poems and poetic prose, both from established and emerging voices. They desire to give the block, the paragraph, the unlineated prose, a new place to play.

- Vending Machine Press – Vending Machine Press (VMP) is aimed at giving writers an avenue for their writing to reach a wider audience. Watch videos and read the poems and stories of the greatest up and coming writers from all over the world.

- Versal – Versal launched in 2002 to develop a rooted and self-sustaining international literary community in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Over the course of its 12 editions, Versal reached across the globe to spotlight the world's premiere, though perhaps unknown, poets, writers, and artists.

- Whisperings – Folklore, poetry, prose, essays, flash prose and short-fiction as yet written. Paintings, sketches, photography and photographic essays as yet viewed.

- Window Cat Press – Window Cat Press offers a place for emerging artists to share quality work as diverse as our audience. They publish a variety of media: cross-genre, collaborations, slam, etc. in addition to more traditional and widely-accepted forms.

- Works & Days Quarterly – Much as any collection of literature, compilation of music, or group show of visual art is only as strong as its components, Works & Days rises and falls on the strength of its contributors.

- Writer's Ink – Inaugurated in 2008, Writer's Ink has thus far published seven volumes, with hundreds of submissions from around the globe by new and experienced authors writing creatively in all styles and genres – from screenplays to memoirs, feminist poetry to steampunk, war stories to haikus – we strive to seek out and promote those works which are distinguished in their quality, originality, and vision.

- Your Impossible Voice – Your Impossible Voice publishes brash and velvety new work from around the globe, as well as translations, literary reviews, essays, and interviews.

- Zizzle Literary Magazine – Zizzle Teens is a new branch of Zizzle Literary specializing in books for teens and young adults.

- ZYZZYVA – ZYZZYVA was founded in 1985 in San Francisco with the goal of publishing a superb literary journal shining a spotlight on West Coast poets, writers, and artists from a wide range of backgrounds, many of whom were otherwise overlooked by established publications, and providing them with a much needed platform.
